title: Almost persuaded (Acts 25–26)
hook: before King Agrippa, Paul: I would that you were as I am, except these chains
tomorrow: fourteen days, no sun, no stars. who gives the pep talk?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Felix trembled at talk of justice and self-control, then said: another time. The line was a convenient season.

Some people hear your whole story and say, that's a lot, maybe later. Paul has heard that before. Now he's brought out before a king, and Acts brings the room in with great pomp: King Agrippa and Bernice, the chief captains, the principal men of the city. The governor, Festus, has a prisoner he can't explain. The king says, "Thou art permitted to speak for thyself." Paul stretches out his hand and tells it all again: the road, the light, the voice. Halfway through, the governor cuts in. Loudly.
screen: `MAYBE LATER.` → `GREAT POMP, AND A PRISONER.` → `THE GOVERNOR CUTS IN.`

segments.voice: Festus shouts, "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad." Paul stays calm: "I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness." Then he turns to the king. You know these things, he says, "for this thing was not done in a corner." And Agrippa answers with the line this day is named for: "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." Some readers hear a king nearly won over. Others hear a dry brush-off: you think you'll make me a Christian that fast? Acts doesn't say which. What it keeps is Paul's reply: "I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds." He wishes them everything he has: the hope, the road, the light. Everything except the chains on his own wrists. No last argument. A wish, said out loud, and left there. Then the king rises, the room empties, and away from the crowd the officials agree: "This man doeth nothing worthy of death or of bonds."
screen: `THOU ART BESIDE THYSELF.` · `NOT DONE IN A CORNER.` · `ALMOST THOU PERSUADEST ME.` · `EVERYTHING, EXCEPT THE CHAINS.` · then, large: `EXCEPT THESE CHAINS.`

segments.voice: Take a scrap of paper. Write one person's name, and under it one good thing you'd wish for them, the way Paul wished his hope on a king. Fold it, set it aside with no plan to persuade anyone, and sit with the wish.
Almost persuaded. A king's half-step toward Paul's story, and Paul's answer: every good thing, and none of the chains.
Your line: except these chains. A good wish, with no pressure in it. That's today, done.

fork.setup: your cousin hears you talk about something that changed you and says, 'almost, but not for me.' what does Paul's answer to Agrippa model?
options: give one more argument while you still have her attention.
wish her every good thing, say so, and leave it there.
drop it, and quietly decide she isn't open to anything.
fork.reveal: Paul doesn't press the king again. he says what he wishes for him, everything except the chains, and the room empties.

original.note: Greek: in a little. readers differ on whether Agrippa means almost, or in so short a time.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king who almost became a Christian.
what it means: a line read two ways, and a prisoner's answer that wishes his hope on everyone without pressing it.
what a scholar hears: ἐν ὀλίγῳ, 'in a little', in 26:28, which can mean almost or in so short a time; Paul's reply in 26:29 picks up the same phrase.

notes: Recipe v3, story shape: the hook drops into the hearing and ends on Festus cutting in; the teach answers it.
The index carry says 'except these chains'; the KJV of Acts 26:29 reads 'except these bonds'. The lesson quotes the KJV and keeps the carry as the index has it. Confirm.
'Great pomp', 'the chief captains' and 'the principal men of the city' are from Acts 25:23 (KJV), paraphrased in the hook.

Acts 26:28 is read two ways (nearly persuaded, or an ironic 'in so short a time'); the lesson says 'some readers' and does not choose. Trapdoor: 26:29 picks up ἐν ὀλίγῳ (καὶ ἐν ὀλίγῳ καὶ ἐν μεγάλῳ); confirm.
Gloss for Festus ('after Felix') rests on Acts 24:27; Bernice is glossed only as she appears in 25:13.
